executive_summary: Today's intelligence picture is dominated by two reinforcing themes: great power competition playing out across technological, economic, and physical domains, and a widening gap between the threats being prioritized and those actively materializing. The US-China AI export controls and Russia's labor crisis both reflect the compounding costs of sustained strategic competition, but the more urgent operational concern is the confirmed Iranian infrastructure campaign targeting water utilities across at least seven states, which represents a live, multi-state attack on critical infrastructure rather than a hypothetical scenario. The FBI/EPA advisory on PLC targeting and the flagged OT supply chain vulnerabilities in the energy sector suggest the water utility intrusions may be the visible edge of a broader effort against internet-exposed operational technology, and the acceleration of digitalization is expanding that attack surface faster than defenses are being applied. The analyst warning that AI-bioweapons hypotheticals are crowding out real unconventional threats is pointed and timely given today's reporting, as the most concrete danger in front of us is not speculative but kinetic and already underway against civilian systems.

sections.title: Geopolitical
sections.intro: Today's geopolitical landscape is defined by intensifying US-China technology competition, distorted weapons policy discourse, and the structural strains of prolonged conflict on Russia's economy.

items.headline: Washington moves to block China from leveraging US AI models as the foundation for its own systems
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Bessent's sanctions threat follows evidence of US model watermarks embedded in Chinese AI outputs, suggesting systematic reverse-engineering or data theft. The policy debate is accelerating rapidly as open-weight models make enforcement increasingly difficult. Watch for whether the administration can develop a technically coherent enforcement mechanism before Chinese labs further close the capability gap.

items.headline: Analysts warn that hypothetical AI-bioweapons scenarios are crowding out real unconventional threats
items.summary: While policy attention fixates on speculative AI-enabled bioweapons, concrete threats — Russian use of chloropicrin in Ukraine and China's evolving biological warfare doctrine — are receiving insufficient scrutiny. The distortion carries strategic risk: misallocated resources and delayed responses to present-day unconventional weapon use. The argument is a call for threat prioritization grounded in observed behavior rather than worst-case extrapolation.

items.headline: Russia's wartime labor crisis deepens as military-industrial expansion cannibalizes the civilian workforce
items.summary: Russia faces a compounding demographic and economic problem: a pre-existing labor shortage is being worsened by military mobilization and the diversion of workers into defense production. This creates inflationary pressure, reduces civilian output, and may constrain Russia's long-term war-sustaining capacity. The structural damage to the Russian economy could outlast the conflict itself, shaping the post-war balance of power.

sections.title: Military
sections.intro: Today's military picture is relatively quiet, with a notable leadership accountability action in the submarine force and low-signal noise elsewhere.

items.headline: Navy fires USS West Virginia submarine commander over loss of confidence
items.summary: Commander Joseph Sammur was relieved of command of the Ohio-class ballistic missile submarine USS West Virginia's Blue Crew, which he had led since August 2025. The Navy cited 'loss of confidence' — a standard but serious basis for relief that typically signals a breakdown in command climate, judgment, or performance. Watch for follow-on reporting on the specific circumstances, as command reliefs on nuclear-armed submarines carry heightened institutional scrutiny.

sections.title: ICS / SCADA / OT
sections.intro: Iran-linked attacks on U.S. water infrastructure are wider than previously reported, prompting joint federal warnings as energy sector OT supply chain risks also draw analyst attention.

items.headline: Iran-linked water utility attacks confirmed across at least seven U.S. states
items.summary: Cyber intrusions targeting water systems have been identified in Michigan, South Dakota, Georgia, and at least four other states beyond the initially reported Minnesota incidents, with Iran-linked threat actors behind the campaign. The geographic breadth signals a coordinated effort against a critical infrastructure sector with historically weak cyber defenses. Watch for attribution updates and whether any attacks resulted in physical operational impact beyond disruption.

items.headline: FBI and EPA issue joint advisory on PLC targeting at internet-exposed water utilities
items.summary: The FBI and EPA have formally warned that threat actors are actively compromising internet-connected programmable logic controllers at U.S. water and wastewater facilities, causing operational disruptions. The advisory underscores a persistent failure by smaller utilities to isolate OT assets from public-facing networks, a known but unresolved vulnerability. The joint federal posture suggests the threat is assessed as serious enough to warrant coordinated public pressure on operators.

items.headline: Analyst firm flags energy sector OT supply chain exposure as digitalization accelerates
items.summary: GlobalData is warning energy companies that grid modernization and the integration of distributed energy resources are expanding OT attack surfaces faster than security investments are scaling to match. Supply chain compromise remains a particularly high-risk vector, as third-party components embedded in OT environments are difficult to audit or patch. Energy firms with ongoing smart grid or DER deployments should treat vendor security posture as a first-order risk factor.
